expressive suppression has a deleterious impact on test performance that persists at one year follow-up in community dwelling older adults.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of expressive suppression (i.e. trying to hide your emotions, such as sadness, anger, etc.) before taking an executive function task (i.e. a task that involves planning, organizing, and decision making) can interfere with the benefits of exposure to that task (i.e., learning from the task), and thereby negatively affecting future executive function performance.
expressive suppression is a strategy that people use to regulate their emotions, and that this strategy can interfere with cognitive performance.
suppression of emotions can interfere with learning and memory, and that it can be particularly detrimental to the learning of complex tasks, which may require the use of executive functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it’s really important to be aware of your emotions, and to know that if you’re feeling upset about something, it might be best to wait to take a test until you’ve had a chance to process your emotions.
expressive suppression is an inefficient emotion regulation strategy, especially for older adults.
